title: Cisco is letting a 27-year-old rewrite 98% of its legacy code with AI: 'Go nuts'
content:
Gen Z can’t catch a break. Entry-level jobs are vanishing; some 40% of bosses say they plan to hire fewer grads because AI can do the job cheaper, and young workers are routinely slammed for showing up late and refusing to put in overtime for free. Cisco’s president and chief product officer Jeetu Patel isn’t buying it—he’s just handed one of the company’s biggest jobs to a 27-year-old he found hidden in the org chart “five levels” below him.
“I’ve given him unlimited tokens because he’s going to refactor code,” Patel told Fortune at a small roundtable dinner. “So I’m like, you can go, you can go nuts.”
The “him” is Padmanabhan Krishnamurthy, or “Paddy,” as Patel affectionately calls him. He joined Cisco in 2025 after the $429 billion tech giant acquired EzDubs, the real-time translation startup Krishnamurthy cofounded in 2023. And despite coming in as a former founder with CEO experience, he was, in Patel’s words, “buried away in the organization doing something unstrategic.”
That changed when Patel dropped into Cisco’s San Francisco office, and the pair got talking. Krishnamurthy reckoned he could rewrite Cisco’s legacy code with a two-person team. Patel says even the most AI-forward people on his own team weren’t thinking that way.
So he has given himself four weeks to prove it, with the final goal of rewriting 98% of Cisco’s legacy code within 24 months.
Now, he’s on the hunt for more Paddys: young hires who will “challenge the system and the status quo,” or, as he puts it, be “an energizer bunny that just goes out and kind of revs everyone up.”
Cisco’s president says Gen Z should be teaching his veterans, not doing data entry—and he’s fine with the tension that causes
At most companies, only someone with decades of experience under their belt would be trusted with a project this size. Patel thinks that’s a problem.
“If you don’t hire the early-in-career [workers], and you just let your workforce continue the way that they were, where do fresh ideas get injected? How do you challenge the status quo?” he said.
Seasoned staff can still come up with new ideas, Patel added. What they can’t do is ask the questions that only someone with no experience would think to ask.
And getting the two to get along isn’t always smooth. Patel admits that putting a Gen Zer in a room with people who’ve been at Cisco for decades can create friction—but he says that’s the point.
“Tension is good,” he said. “I actually try to create tension in the teams because you want to have enough friction on the ideas. You don’t want to have friction with people and personalities.”
“What you have to do is establish enough trust with people to say you are going to be expected to create unreasonable goals for yourself,” he added. “And so, in order to go out and achieve those unreasonable goals, think outside of the box.”
And he’s not just pushing senior staff to take notes from twentysomethings. He said that he treats every intern as “kind of a reverse mentor,” and even does talks at colleges to find students who are “hungry.”
His latest Gen Z bet came out of one of those talks, to 17- and 18-year-old Stanford scholarship students. While a line of students fired questions at him, one, Baya, stood off to the side, just listening. She waited until everyone else had finished before she opened up.
He told her to email him every month with what she’d learned about AI. It was a test of follow-through: “Everyone can go out and have one good conversation. But are they going to stick with their commitments?”
She never missed one, landed an internship at Cisco, and redesigned “something” that experienced staff hadn’t been able to crack.
“I didn’t bring her in so that she can do grunt work and do data entry,” he said. “We brought her in so that she could actually teach our people how to think completely differently.” Now he wants to recruit her.
Patel isn’t the only one betting on Gen Z—OpenAI investor Josh Kushner and Will.i.am are hunting for young, hungry talent
Patel isn’t the only boss who sees Gen Z’s lack of experience as an asset.
Thrive Capital’s founder Josh Kushner told Fortune he specifically likes to hire people with less than four years of industry experience.
When he launched the venture capital firm at just 26, he faced pressure to bring in older, more seasoned hires. But, as he put it, “anyone who has experience that is talented will never want to work with a 26-year-old.” So, instead, he recruited the “smartest people that we knew who were our ages.”
And that bet paid off: His firm made early investments in startups worth billions, including OpenAI, which is currently raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation.
These days, Kushner could easily hire industry veterans with glowing résumés—but he’d still rather “find that young, hungry person.”
Alon Chen, founder and CEO of Tastewise—a generative AI platform trusted by PepsiCo, Nestlé, and Mars—is also actively looking for Gen Zers with zero experience.
“I’m hiring entry-level because they have no boundaries or limitations in how they think about the world,” Chen told Fortune. “They’re almost like AI natives themselves, having been born and raised in this new realm of opportunities. And I see some of the best ideas coming from the younger generation that have not yet been in the job market.”
And Will.i.am has reached a similar conclusion. The Grammy-winning Black Eyed Peas frontman might be best known for his chart-topping hits, but behind the scenes, he’s a serious investor too. He backed Tesla, OpenAI, and Pinterest before they became household names—and now, he’s betting on Gen Z for his next investment.
Why? He believes the next big tech breakthroughs will come from young innovators at MIT and Stanford. “They’re young kids, and they’re native to this,” Will.i.am told Fortune. “So you want to hunt for that. That’s the only thing I’m focused on.”
And Patel told Fortune that the trend toward hiring Gen Z will only continue, thanks to AI.
“The only way for us to keep accelerating is to make sure we’re surrounded by people with a broad range of experience,” he said. “Roughly one-third of my team is experienced, scaled operators who understand how the Cisco engine works. The second third are systems thinkers from the market who bring the outside-in perspective. And the final third is made of entrepreneurial founders, CEOs, and engineers who are AI-native who operate in founder mode.”
“Either of these groups by themselves aren’t nearly as potent as when all three work together. It’s what creates magic.”

report.summary: Cisco president Jeetu Patel has given a 27-year-old engineer unlimited AI tokens to lead an ambitious effort to rewrite 98% of Cisco’s legacy code within 24 months.
report.background: Cisco’s plan lands amid a broader reckoning over legacy code, AI-assisted software development and entry-level hiring. Large enterprises run critical systems on decades-old code that is costly to maintain and risky to replace. Generative AI coding agents now promise to accelerate refactoring, testing and documentation, but most firms are still experimenting. At the same time, AI is absorbing many tasks historically assigned to junior developers, prompting some executives to cut graduate hiring. Cisco acquired EzDubs in 2025, bringing Krishnamurthy into the company. Patel’s bet reflects a counterargument: young AI-native workers can challenge entrenched assumptions, while experienced operators provide institutional knowledge. The experiment tests whether unlimited AI tokens and a small, founder-style team can modernize a $429 billion company’s core systems faster than conventional engineering programs.
key_points: Cisco president Jeetu Patel has handed Padmanabhan 'Paddy' Krishnamurthy, a 27-year-old EzDubs cofounder, unlimited AI tokens and a two-person team. Krishnamurthy has four weeks to prove he can refactor Cisco’s legacy code, with a target of rewriting 98% within 24 months. Patel says even AI-forward colleagues were not thinking that aggressively.

Patel is deliberately recruiting early-career workers and treating interns as reverse mentors. He wants Gen Z employees to ask naive but valuable questions and challenge status quo assumptions. Putting twentysomethings alongside decades-long Cisco veterans creates friction, which Patel says is intentional: tension over ideas is useful, but personal friction is not.

The article ties Cisco’s bet to a wider talent shift. Thrive Capital’s Josh Kushner, Tastewise CEO Alon Chen and investor will.i.am all say they prize young, AI-native hires over purely experienced candidates. They argue that people with less industry experience have fewer boundaries and often generate ideas that veterans miss.

The backdrop is anxiety about entry-level jobs. About 40% of bosses reportedly plan to hire fewer graduates because AI can do the work cheaper. Patel rejects that logic, arguing that companies that stop hiring young workers lose fresh ideas and the ability to challenge the status quo. His answer is to give them unusually large responsibilities.

Patel describes a three-part team model: experienced operators who understand Cisco, outside systems thinkers, and founder-mode AI-native engineers. He says none of the groups is as potent alone as when combined. The Cisco experiment is therefore as much about organizational design and talent mixing as about AI coding tools.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Cisco’s experiment is a high-profile test of whether coding agents can safely modernize massive legacy estates, not just write snippets. Success would strengthen the case for unlimited-token, agent-driven refactoring; failure would expose limits around code quality, security, testing and institutional knowledge. For developers, it signals that junior roles may shift from grunt work to questioning systems and orchestrating AI, while seniors must mentor and validate machine output. For regular users, faster modernization could mean more reliable and secure services, but rushed AI rewrites carry outage and data-risk concerns. The bigger lesson is organizational: AI-native talent and veteran expertise must be deliberately combined.
report.tools: Watch AI coding agents such as OpenAI Codex, Anthropic’s Claude Code, GitHub Copilot and Cursor; open-source options include Aider, OpenHands, SWE-agent and Continue. For legacy analysis, pair them with CodeQL, SonarQube and dependency scanners. The key follow-up is not just which model writes code, but how teams test, review and govern large-scale refactors.
